## Definition

For exposure $e\ge0$ and rate $\lambda>0$, define
$Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(e\lambda)$ to have [[def-scalar-poisson-count-law|the scalar Poisson count law]] with
parameter $e\lambda$. Thus for $e>0$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=y\mid\lambda,e)=e^{-e\lambda}\frac{(e\lambda)^y}{y!}, \qquad y\in\mathbb N_0,$$
with $0^0=1$; when $e=0$ this is the point mass at $y=0$. The law is normalized
by [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. A zero-exposure
positive count has likelihood zero.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. For shape $a>0$ and rate $b>0$, the **shape-rate Gamma distribution**
$\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ is the probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ with
density
$$f_{a,b}(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. Its normalization is proved in
[[lem-gamma-density-normalization]]. The second argument is a rate, not a scale.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $a,b>0$,
$$\int_{(0,\infty)}\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx}\,d\lambda_1(x)=1.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and positive real parameters $a,b$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom required by the bounded-Riemann-to-Lebesgue integral and Lebesgue change-of-variables suppliers. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] $\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ as a mixed improper integral. [[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]].

[F2] This Euler integral is finite and strictly positive for $a>0$. [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

[F3] Bounded Riemann-integrable functions on compact intervals have the same Lebesgue integral. [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]].

[F4] A continuous function on a compact interval is bounded and Riemann integrable. [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]].

[F5] Monotone convergence holds for nonnegative measurable functions. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]].

[F6] For a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open sets, Lebesgue change of variables holds for nonnegative measurable functions under Countable Choice. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F7] Positive real powers and the real exponential are continuous on their domains. [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]].

[F8] Integration is with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure. [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and $a,b>0$.

1.1 By [F7], $g(t)=t^{a-1}e^{-t}$ is continuous and hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable on $(0,\infty)$ with the measure in [F8]. For each integer $m\ge2$, its restriction to $[1/m,m]$ is continuous, hence bounded Riemann integrable by [F4], and [F3] identifies its Riemann integral with its Lebesgue integral. The truncated functions $g\,\mathbf1_{[1/m,m]}$ increase to $g$. [A1, F3, F4, F7, F8, construct]

2.1 Monotone convergence [F5] identifies $\int g\,d\lambda_1$ with the limit of those truncated integrals. By the mixed-improper-integral definition [F1] and convergence [F2], this limit is $\Gamma(a)$, so $g$ has finite positive Lebesgue integral. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F5]

3.1 Apply [F6] to the diffeomorphism $t=bx$ of $(0,\infty)$. Since $dt=b\,dx$ and $x=t/b$, it gives $\int_0^\infty x^{a-1}e^{-bx}\,dx=b^{-a}\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt=b^{-a}\Gamma(a).$ Multiplication by $b^a/\Gamma(a)$ is valid by [F2] and yields one. [A1, F2, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For $k\ge2$ and positive coordinates $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k$, write
$\Delta_{k-1}=\{(p_1,\ldots,p_{k-1})\in(0,\infty)^{k-1}:
\sum_{j<k}p_j<1\}$ and set $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. The **Dirichlet density
kernel** is the nonnegative function
$$q_\alpha(p_1,\ldots,p_{k-1}) =\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j-1},\qquad \alpha_+=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j,$$
relative to coordinate Lebesgue measure $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$. This item
defines the density function.

## Remarks

[[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]] proves that this kernel integrates to
one.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$,
$$\int_{\Delta_{k-1}}\prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j-1}\,dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1} =\frac{\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}\in(0,\infty).$$
Consequently the density kernel in [[def-dirichlet-density-kernel]] has
integral one.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $k\ge2$, and $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k>0$.

[A1] Countable Choice is required for the stated nonnegative Lebesgue change-of-variables theorem. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The simplex and its nonnegative density kernel are defined in coordinate Lebesgue measure by [[def-dirichlet-density-kernel]].

[F2] A $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open sets changes variables in a nonnegative Lebesgue integral under Countable Choice. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F3] Tonelli factors a nonnegative product integral over a finite sigma-finite product space into iterated integrals. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F4] For $u,v>0$, the one-dimensional Beta integrand has Lebesgue integral $B(u,v)=\Gamma(u)\Gamma(v)/\Gamma(u+v)$, finite and positive. [[lem-beta-density-normalization]].

[F5] The Beta-Gamma identity holds for positive arguments. [[thm-real-beta-gamma-identity]].

[F6] Gamma values at positive arguments are finite and positive. [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice, $k\ge2$, and positive $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k$.

1.1 Define the stick-breaking map from $(0,1)^{k-1}$ to $\Delta_{k-1}$ by $p_i=z_i\prod_{j<i}(1-z_j)$ for $i<k$. Its inverse is $z_i=p_i/(1-\sum_{j<i}p_j)$, so it is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. Its derivative matrix is lower triangular with diagonal entries $\prod_{j<i}(1-z_j)$; hence its Jacobian is $\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}(1-z_i)^{k-i-1}$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Under this change of variables, each factor $p_j^{\alpha_j-1}$ contributes $z_j^{\alpha_j-1}$ and a factor $(1-z_i)^{\alpha_j-1}$ for each $i<j$; the Jacobian adds exponent $k-i-1$ to $1-z_i$. Thus the transformed integrand is $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}z_i^{\alpha_i-1} (1-z_i)^{\sum_{j>i}\alpha_j-1}.$ This factorization is valid because all coordinates and residuals are strictly positive on the open cube. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Tonelli [F3] and [F4] now give the integral as $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}B\!\left(\alpha_i,\sum_{j>i}\alpha_j\right).$ Applying [F5] to each factor cancels the intermediate Gamma terms and leaves $\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)/\Gamma(\alpha_+)$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F6] the displayed ratio is finite and positive. Multiplying the integrand by the reciprocal constant in [F1] therefore gives integral one, which proves normalization. [F1, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,
\alpha_k)$, with each $\alpha_j>0$. Conditional on $p$, observe a
Multinomial$(n,p)$ count vector $y\in\mathbb N_0^k$ with $\sum_jy_j=n$.
For $k\ge2$, the data space is equipped with counting measure on its finite
set of admissible counts. The evidence is
$$m(y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!} \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)} \in(0,\infty),$$
where $\alpha_+=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and the posterior is
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$.
For $k=1$, the parameter and count are both deterministic and the posterior
equals the prior point mass.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, positive $\alpha_j$, $n\ge0$, and admissible
counts $y_j\ge0$ summing to $n$.

[A1] Countable Choice is required by the Dirichlet simplex normalization theorem. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The Dirichlet law has density $\Gamma(\alpha_+)/\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)\prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$ on the open simplex for $k\ge2$, and is a point mass at $1$ for $k=1$. [[def-dirichlet-distribution]].

[F2] The Dirichlet simplex density is normalized by iterated Beta integrals under Countable Choice. [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]].

[F3] The Multinomial$(n,p)$ likelihood is $n!\prod_jp_j^{y_j}/\prod_jy_j!$ and is normalized. [[def-multinomial-distribution]].

[F4] A proper prior and parameter-measurable probability sampling kernel constitute a Bayesian model. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]].

[F5] The evidence is the integral of the likelihood against the prior; no quotient is defined unless it is finite and positive. [[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]].

[F6] A likelihood-weighted prior is a probability after normalization exactly for finite positive evidence. [[prop-fiberwise-posterior-propriety-iff-finite-positive-evidence]].

[F7] The dominated Bayes formula identifies the normalized likelihood quotient as a posterior conditional kernel. [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and observed count vector $y$.

1.1 If $k=1$, then $p_1=1$ and the only admissible count is $y_1=n$. The likelihood and evidence are one, so the point-mass prior is unchanged. Assume henceforth $k\ge2$. Multiplying the prior and likelihood densities [F1, F3] gives a constant times $\prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j+y_j-1},$ with every updated coordinate positive. The finite count space, proper prior, and normalized measurable likelihood give the model in [F4]. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, cases]

2.1 By [F2], the integral of this updated simplex kernel is $\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)/\Gamma(\alpha_++n)$, finite and positive. Multiplying by the prior normalizing constant and the Multinomial coefficient from [F3] yields exactly the displayed evidence. It is finite positive, so [F5] and [F6] place this fiber in the valid update domain. [A1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Divide the product density from step 1.1 by its evidence from step 2.1. The resulting density is $\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)} \prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j+y_j-1},$ the normalized Dirichlet$(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$ density by [F2]. The evidence is positive finite, so [F7] makes this normalized law the posterior conditional kernel. Zero counts leave their coordinates positive and unchanged; no boundary parameter points are introduced. [A1, F2, F5, F7, step 2.1, cases] ∎

## Statement

If $S$ is a nonempty at-most-countable set, then $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is a
standard Borel space.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty at-most-countable set $S$ and its power-set
$\mathcal P(S)$.

[F1] [[def-countable]]: an at-most-countable set is finite or equinumerous
with $\mathbb N$.

[F2] [[def-sigma-algebra]]: a sigma-algebra contains the whole space and is
closed under complements and countable unions.

[F3] [[def-metric-space]]: a metric is a real-valued function that separates
distinct points, is symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality. The
definition does not assume nonnegativity; for the metric constructed below,
nonnegativity follows directly from its two cases.

[F4] [[def-metric-ball]]: an open ball of radius $r>0$ about $s$ is
$B(s,r)=\{t\in S:d(s,t)<r\}$.

[F5] [[def-metric-topology]]: a set is open when every one of its points has
a ball around it contained in the set.

[F6] [[def-cauchy-in-metric]]: a sequence is Cauchy if for every rational
$\epsilon>0$ its terms are pairwise within $\epsilon$ after some index.

[F7] [[def-complete-metric-space]]: a metric space is complete if every
Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.

[F8] [[def-separable-space]]: a space is separable if it has a countable dense
subset.

[F9] [[def-polish-space]]: a topological space is Polish if it is separable
and its topology is induced by a complete metric.

[F10] [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]: the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by
the open sets of a topological space.

[F11] [[def-standard-borel-space]]: a measurable space is standard Borel if
it is measurably isomorphic to a Polish space with its Borel sigma-algebra.

## Proof

1.1 Define $d(s,t)=0$ when $s=t$ and $d(s,t)=1$ when $s\ne t$. These values are nonnegative, the definition is symmetric, and $d(s,t)=0$ exactly when $s=t$. If $s\ne u$, then at least one of $s\ne t$ or $t\ne u$ holds, so $d(s,u)=1\le d(s,t)+d(t,u)$; if $s=u$, the triangle inequality follows from nonnegativity. Thus [F3] makes $d$ a metric. For every $s\in S$, [F4] gives $B(s,1/2)=\{s\}$, so [F5] shows that every subset of $S$ is open. [F3, F4, F5, given]

2.1 If $(s_n)$ is Cauchy, [F6] with the rational $\epsilon=1/2$ gives an index $N$ such that $d(s_m,s_n)<1/2$ for all $m,n\ge N$. Hence all $s_n$ for $n\ge N$ are equal, so the sequence converges in $S$; by [F7], $d$ is complete. Since $S$ is at-most-countable and dense in itself, [F8] makes $(S,d)$ separable. [F6, F7, F8, F1, step 1.1, given]

3.1 The power set is closed under relative complements and countable unions, so it is a sigma-algebra by [F2]. By [F10] and step 1.1, every subset of $S$ belongs to the Borel sigma-algebra. Conversely, every Borel set is a subset of $S$, so this sigma-algebra is exactly $\mathcal P(S)$. Therefore $(S,d)$ is Polish by [F9], and the identity map from $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ to $(S,\mathcal B(S,d))$ is a measurable bijection with measurable inverse. [F2, F10, step 1.1, F9, step 2.1, given]

4.1 The identity map in step 3.1 is a measurable isomorphism to a Polish space, so [F11] gives that $(S,\mathcal P(S))$ is standard Borel. [step 3.1, F11] ∎

## Definition

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite
measure on it. A **counting measure** on $(E,\mathcal E)$ is a measure of the
form $\eta=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{z_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$;
repetitions among the points $z_j$ are allowed. Equip the set
$\mathcal N(E)$ of these measures with the **evaluation sigma-algebra**
generated by the maps $\eta\mapsto\eta(B)$, $B\in\mathcal E$. A random
counting measure is a measurable map from a probability space into
$\mathcal N(E)$.

A **Poisson random measure** with intensity $\nu$ is a random counting
measure $N$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint family
$B_1,\ldots,B_m\in\mathcal E$ with $\nu(B_j)<\infty$, the counts
$N(B_1),\ldots,N(B_m)$ are mutually independent and
$N(B_j)\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\nu(B_j))$. Here
$\operatorname{Pois}(c)$ is the law in [[def-poisson-law]] with exposure
$e=c$ and rate $\lambda=1$, so $c=0$ means the point mass at zero. This
definition imposes no topology, local compactness, or local-finiteness
condition on $E$.

## Definition

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a standard Borel space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and a finite measure $\alpha$ with $0<\alpha(\mathsf X)<\infty$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[A2] Full AC implies Countable Choice, which is the choice strength required by the local Gamma and Dirichlet normalization interfaces. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] Countable products of standard Borel coordinate spaces admit the consistent product law under AC, and finite products remain standard Borel. The countable discrete space $\mathbb N_0$ is standard Borel. [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]] [[def-standard-borel-space]] [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]] [[lem-countable-discrete-space-is-standard-borel]].

[F2] A Poisson count with finite mean $c$ has mass $e^{-c}c^j/j!$ and mean $c$, including the degenerate $c=0$ case. [[def-poisson-law]] [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]].

[F3] Finite product measures satisfy the rectangle product formula, and Tonelli applies to nonnegative functions on their sigma-finite products. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F4] Under Countable Choice, the shape-rate Gamma law has density $x\mapsto x^{a-1}e^{-x}/\Gamma(a)$ at rate $1$, normalized for $a>0$. [[def-gamma-distribution-shape-rate]] [[lem-gamma-density-normalization]].

[F5] For nonnegative measurable functions, Lebesgue change of variables holds under Countable Choice. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F6] The exponential integral and natural logarithm satisfy $\int_0^\infty e^{-ct}dt=1/c$ for $c>0$ and $\int_0^s(1-v)^{-1}dv=-\log(1-s)$ for $s<1$. [[thm-integral-exponential-agrees-with-exponential]] [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]] [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]].

[F7] A finite complex measure on $\mathbb R^k$ with an exponential moment is determined by its Laplace transform on a real neighborhood of zero under AC. [[lem-uniqueness-of-a-multivariate-exponential-transform]].

[F8] A countable nonnegative weighted sum of measures is a measure, and each $\delta_x$ is a probability measure. [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]] [[def-dirac-measure]] [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

[F9] For positive Dirichlet parameters, the simplex density is normalized; the one-category law is the point mass at one. [[def-dirichlet-distribution]] [[def-dirichlet-density-kernel]] [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]].

[F10] Finite measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and the whole space are equal by finite-measure uniqueness and Dynkin's pi-lambda theorem. [[def-pi-system]] [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]].

[F11] Expectations of measurable functions are integrals against the random element's law. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]] [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

[F12] Measurability of random elements is tested against the target sigma-algebra, and their laws are probability measures. [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]] [[def-probability-measure]].

[F13] Finite families of mutually independent random elements have the product joint law. [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]].

[F14] A finite measure is one with finite total mass, and sigma-finiteness is exhaustion by countably many finite-measure sets. [[def-measure]] [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]].

[F15] A law with the finite-partition Dirichlet conditions, when it exists, is denoted $DP(\alpha)$, and there is at most one such law. [[def-dirichlet-process]].

[F16] Monotone convergence passes increasing nonnegative limits through the integral, and dominated convergence applies under an integrable bound. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]] [[thm-dominated-convergence]].

[F17] The Poisson mass formula and the exponential series give $\mathbb E[c^N]=e^{\lambda(c-1)}$ for $c\ge0$ when $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$. [[def-poisson-law]] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]].

[F18] The binomial theorem gives $\sum_{h=0}^k\binom{k}{h}a^hb^{k-h}=(a+b)^k$. [[thm-binomial-theorem]].


[F19] The Euler integral defines $\Gamma(a)$ and is finite and positive for $a>0$. [[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]] [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

[F20] Independence means mutual factorization on measurable rectangles. [[def-independent-random-elements]].

[F21] The usual real line is Polish: the usual metric is complete and the rationals are countable and dense. [[def-polish-space]] [[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] [[thm-rationals-countable]] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]].

[F22] The function $t\mapsto t^{-1}e^{-t}$ is nonnegative and Borel measurable on $(0,\infty)$ because its factors are continuous there. Its integral over Borel sets with respect to Lebesgue measure defines a measure. [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]] [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

[F23] Every Borel subset of a Polish space, with its trace Borel sigma-algebra, is standard Borel under AC. The set $(0,\infty)$ is open in the usual real line, hence Borel; apply [F21]. [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put $\rho(dt)=t^{-1}e^{-t}dt$ on $(0,\infty)$; [F22] makes this a measure with a nonnegative density, relative to Lebesgue measure, and partition the mark axis into $I_0=[1,\infty)$ and $I_m=[1/(m+1),1/m)$ for $m\ge1$. These disjoint strips cover $(0,\infty)$. For $m\ge1$, $\rho(I_m)\le 1/m$ because $t^{-1}\le m+1$ and $e^{-t}\le1$ there, while $\rho(I_m)\ge1/(e(m+1))>0$ because $t^{-1}\ge m$, $e^{-t}\ge e^{-1}$, and the interval length is $1/(m(m+1))$. Also $\rho(I_0)\le\int_1^\infty e^{-t}dt<\infty$ and $\rho(I_0)\ge e^{-2}/2>0$ by restricting to $[1,2]$. Thus every strip has finite positive mass. By [F3] and [F14], $\mu=\alpha\otimes\rho$ is sigma-finite and $\mu_m:=\mu|_{\mathsf X\times I_m}$ has finite positive total $\lambda_m=\alpha(\mathsf X)\rho(I_m)$. Let $Q_m=\mu_m/\lambda_m$. [given, F3, F6, F14, F22, construct]

2.1 Index count coordinates by $m\ge0$ and mark coordinates by $(m,\ell)$ with $m\ge0,\ell\ge1$. Their spaces are $\mathbb N_0$ and $\mathsf X\times(0,\infty)$, respectively, hence standard Borel by [F1], [F21], and [F23]. Assign every finite set of coordinates the product of the laws $\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_m)$ and $Q_m$. These finite-dimensional laws are consistent because coordinate projections of a finite product recover the corresponding marginal products. By [F1] and [A1] they extend to one probability law. The product rectangle formula gives mutual independence of each finite coordinate family by [F20], and [F13] identifies its joint law with the product. Thus it supports mutually independent $N_m\sim \operatorname{Pois}(\lambda_m)$ and $Z_{m\ell}=(X_{m\ell},T_{m\ell})\sim Q_m$. [A1, F1, F3, F13, F20, F21, F23, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Define $N=\sum_{m\ge0}\sum_{\ell\ge1}\mathbf1_{\{\ell\le N_m\}}\delta_{Z_{m\ell}}$. Each $N_m$ is finite, so this is a countable sum of Dirac measures and is a counting measure by [F8]. For every measurable $B$, its evaluation is the increasing limit of finite sums of measurable functions of the coordinates; hence $N(B)$ is measurable. Thus $N$ is a random counting measure. [F8, F12, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 Fix pairwise-disjoint measurable sets $B_1,\ldots,B_r$ with $\mu(B_j)<\infty$. Within strip $m$, put $q_{jm}=Q_m(B_j)$ and $q_{0m}=1-\sum_{j=1}^r q_{jm}$. Conditional on $N_m=n$, independent marks assign counts $(k_0,k_1,\ldots,k_r)$ with $n=k_0+\cdots+k_r$. There are $n!/\prod_{j=0}^r k_j!$ assignments of the $n$ mark indices to these cells, and each assignment has probability $\prod_{j=0}^r q_{jm}^{k_j}$, so the count vector has mass $n!\prod_{j=0}^r q_{jm}^{k_j}/\prod_{j=0}^r k_j!$ (with $0^0=1$). Summing over $k_0$ and using the Poisson mass in [F2] gives $\Pr\{N_m(B_j)=k_j,\ 1\le j\le r\}=e^{-\lambda_m}\bigl(\prod_{j=1}^r(\lambda_mq_{jm})^{k_j}/k_j!\bigr)e^{\lambda_mq_{0m}}=\prod_{j=1}^r e^{-\mu_m(B_j)}\mu_m(B_j)^{k_j}/k_j!$; here $\lambda_mq_{jm}=\mu_m(B_j)$ and $\lambda_m(1-q_{0m})=\sum_j\mu_m(B_j)$. Thus the strip counts are independent Poisson variables with means $\mu_m(B_j)$. The series over $k_0$ is the exponential series [F17]. [F2, F17, F22, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 Define $\Gamma(A)=\sum_{m\ge0}\sum_{\ell\ge1} \mathbf1_{\{\ell\le N_m\}}T_{m\ell}\mathbf1_{\{X_{m\ell}\in A\}}$ for $A\in\mathcal A$. This is a measurable nonnegative weighted sum of Dirac measures, hence a measure by [F8]. For each strip, independence of $N_m$ and its marks [F13], expectation against their law [F11], and $\mathbb E N_m=\lambda_m$ from [F2] give $\mathbb E\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_m}T_{m\ell}\mathbf1_{\{X_{m\ell}\in A\}} =\lambda_m\int t\mathbf1_A(x)\,Q_m(dx,dt) =\int_{A\times I_m}t\,\mu(dx,dt)$. Monotone convergence [F16] then gives $\mathbb E\Gamma(A)=\sum_m\int_{A\times I_m}t\,\mu(dx,dt) =\alpha(A)\int_0^\infty e^{-t}dt=\alpha(A)$ by [F3] and [F6]. [F2, F3, F6, F8, F11, F13, F16, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.4 Let $A_1,\ldots,A_r$ be pairwise disjoint and choose $|u_j|<\delta<1$. On strip $m$, define $g_m(x,t)=\sum_{j=1}^r e^{u_jt}\mathbf1_{A_j}(x) +\mathbf1_{\mathsf X\setminus\cup_jA_j}(x)$. Conditional on $N_m=n$, the independent marks give the exponential factor $(\int g_m\,dQ_m)^n$. Summing its Poisson series yields $\mathbb E\exp(\sum_j u_j\Gamma_M(A_j)) =\exp(\sum_j\alpha(A_j)\int_{\cup_{m\le M}I_m} (e^{u_jt}-1)\rho(dt))$, where $\Gamma_M$ sums the first $M+1$ strips. The mark integral is finite on each strip because the strips are bounded away from zero and $u_j<1$; the Poisson series is [F17]. [F2, F17, F22, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For each finite $M$, the sums over $m\le M$ are independent Poisson counts: convolution and [F18] give $\sum_{h=0}^k e^{-a}a^h/h!\,e^{-b}b^{k-h}/(k-h)! =e^{-(a+b)}(a+b)^k/k!$, and iteration handles $M$. By [F16], their increasing total counts have $\mathbb E N(B_j)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\sum_{m\le M}\mu_m(B_j)=\mu(B_j)<\infty$. Thus the full counts are finite almost surely and the truncated integer counts eventually stabilize. Their joint point probabilities converge both to the point probabilities of the full count vector (by eventual stabilization) and to the product Poisson masses with means $\mu(B_j)$ (by continuity of the Poisson mass formula in its mean). Hence the full counts are independent Poisson variables with means $\mu(B_j)$. Therefore $N$ satisfies [[def-poisson-random-measure]]. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.2, F2, F16, F18, algebra]

4.2 Since $\mathbb E\Gamma(\mathsf X)=\alpha(\mathsf X)<\infty$, $\Gamma(\mathsf X)<\infty$ almost surely: if it were infinite on a set of positive probability, its expectation would exceed every finite bound. Also, $\Gamma(A)$ is measurable for every $A$ as a monotone limit of finite coordinate sums. [given, F11, F12, step 3.3]

4.3 For $u<1$, $\int_0^\infty(e^{ut}-1)t^{-1}e^{-t}dt =\int_0^u(1-v)^{-1}dv=-\log(1-u)$: use $(e^{ut}-1)/t=\int_0^u e^{vt}dv$, Tonelli on the positive or negative part, and [F6]. In particular $\mathbb E e^{\delta\Gamma(\mathsf X)} =(1-\delta)^{-\alpha(\mathsf X)}<\infty$, by monotone convergence [F16] on the nonnegative truncations. For general $|u_j|<\delta$, the truncated exponentials are dominated by $e^{\delta\Gamma(\mathsf X)}$; [F16] therefore gives $\mathbb E e^{\sum_j u_j\Gamma(A_j)} =\prod_j(1-u_j)^{-\alpha(A_j)}$. [F3, F6, F16, F22, step 1.1, step 3.3, step 3.4, algebra]

5.1 Let $J_+=\{j: \alpha(A_j)>0\}$. For $j\in J_+$, [F4], [F5], and the Euler integral [F19], with $t=(1-u)y$, give $\mathbb E e^{uY}=\Gamma(a)^{-1}\int_0^\infty y^{a-1}e^{-(1-u)y}dy=(1-u)^{-a}$ for $Y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a,1)$ and $u<1$. Thus the vector $(\Gamma(A_j))_{j\in J_+}$ and the product of the corresponding Gamma laws have the same moment-generating transform near zero by step 4.3; [F3] supplies that finite product law, and [F7] identifies the distributions when $J_+$ is nonempty; if $J_+$ is empty this clause is vacuous. For each $j\notin J_+$, step 3.3 gives $\mathbb E\Gamma(A_j)=0$. If $\Gamma(A_j)>0$ with positive probability, some event $\{\Gamma(A_j)\ge1/q\}$ has positive probability, forcing its nonnegative expectation to be positive; hence $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely. Since there are finitely many cells, these zero coordinates are simultaneously zero almost surely. Their events in any measurable rectangle have probability zero or one, so adjoining these constants preserves the product law and independence. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F7, F19, step 3.3, step 4.3, cases, algebra]

6.1 For a partition with $r\ge2$ positive cells and parameters $a_1,\ldots,a_r$, the independent Gamma increments have product density $\prod_j z_j^{a_j-1}e^{-z_j}/\Gamma(a_j)$. Change variables to $s=\sum_j z_j$ and $p_j=z_j/s$ for $j<r$, with $p_r=1-\sum_{j<r}p_j$. Its Jacobian has absolute value $s^{r-1}$: factor $s$ from each of the $r-1$ proportion columns, then add the first $r-1$ rows of the remaining matrix to its last row, whose first entry becomes $\sum_jp_j=1$ and whose other entries become zero. The inverse map is $s=\sum_jz_j$, $p_j=z_j/s$, so this is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism on the positive orthant and open simplex. The joint density factors as the Gamma$(\sum_j a_j,1)$ density in $s$ times $\Gamma(\sum_j a_j)\prod_jp_j^{a_j-1}/\prod_j\Gamma(a_j)$ on the simplex. Integrating the normalized Gamma factor in $s$, which has total mass one by [F4], leaves the second factor as the marginal density of $p$. By [F9] this is the Dirichlet law. With one positive cell the normalized mass is one, and zero-base cells have zero mass by step 5.1. [A2, F5, F4, F9, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The total $\Gamma(\mathsf X)$ is Gamma$(\alpha(\mathsf X),1)$ by step 5.1, so it is strictly positive almost surely; step 4.2 gives finiteness. Since $\alpha(\mathsf X)>0$, the space $\mathsf X$ is nonempty; choose $x_0\in\mathsf X$ and set $G(A)=\Gamma(A)/\Gamma(\mathsf X)$ on that probability-one event, assigning $\delta_{x_0}$ on its null complement. The event is measurable and each evaluation $G(A)$ is measurable, so [F12] makes $G$ a random probability measure with the partition laws from step 6.1. [given, F8, F12, step 4.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, choose, construct]

8.1 Finite evaluation cylinders form a generating pi-system for the evaluation sigma-algebra. For any $A_1,\ldots,A_s\in\mathcal A$, the nonempty intersections of $A_i$ and $A_i^c$ form a finite partition, and each $G(A_i)$ is the sum of the corresponding cell masses. Hence its joint law is fixed by step 6.1. Two probability laws with those partition laws therefore agree on the generating pi-system; [F10] gives equality on the entire evaluation sigma-algebra. By [F15], this is uniqueness of $DP(\alpha)$. [F10, F15, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $P=(P_1,\ldots,P_k)$ have the Dirichlet distribution with
positive parameters $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$. If
$I_1,\ldots,I_r$ is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ into nonempty groups,
then
$$\left(\sum_{j\in I_1}P_j,\ldots,\sum_{j\in I_r}P_j\right)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(b_1,\ldots,b_r),\qquad b_\ell=\sum_{j\in I_\ell}a_j.$$
When $r=1$, the grouped vector is the point mass at $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; positive $a_1,\ldots,a_k$; and a partition of the coordinate indices into nonempty groups.

[A1] Full AC is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[A2] Full AC implies the Countable Choice required by Gamma density normalization. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] On a finite discrete standard Borel space, the normalized-gamma construction realizes a positive-parameter Dirichlet vector as independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(a_j,1)$ increments divided by their sum. [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]].

[F2] Under Countable Choice, a shape-rate Gamma$(a,1)$ variable has density $z^{a-1}e^{-z}/\Gamma(a)$, normalized for $a>0$; the Euler Gamma value is finite and positive. [[def-gamma-distribution-shape-rate]] [[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]] [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

[F3] Under Countable Choice, the nonnegative Lebesgue change-of-variables formula holds for $C^1$ diffeomorphisms. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F4] Finite measures with an exponential moment and the same Laplace transform on a neighborhood of zero are equal under AC. [[lem-uniqueness-of-a-multivariate-exponential-transform]].

[F5] Finite products of probability measures exist and satisfy the rectangle product formula. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

[F6] The finite-dimensional Dirichlet law is the positive-parameter simplex law specified in [[def-dirichlet-distribution]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Apply [F1] to the finite discrete space $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ with base masses $a_j$. Thus the law of $P$ is that of $Z_j/\sum_{h=1}^kZ_h$, where the $Z_j$ are independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(a_j,1)$ variables, and it is the Dirichlet law [F6]. [A1, F1, F5, F6, given, construct]

2.1 For $u<1$, [F2] and the change of variables $t=(1-u)z$ in [F3] give $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=\Gamma(a_j)^{-1}\int_0^\infty z^{a_j-1}e^{-(1-u)z}dz=(1-u)^{-a_j}$. For $W_\ell=\sum_{j\in I_\ell}Z_j$, independence therefore gives the joint moment-generating function $\prod_{\ell=1}^r(1-u_\ell)^{-b_\ell}$ for $|u_\ell|<\delta<1$, since the groups use disjoint coordinates in the finite product law [F5]. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F5], the product law of independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(b_\ell,1)$ variables exists and has the same joint transform. Both laws have finite exponential moment at every $0<\delta<1$, since the transform at $(\delta,\ldots,\delta)$ is finite. Applying [F4] to the difference of these two finite measures shows that $(W_1,\ldots,W_r)$ has that product Gamma law. [A1, A2, F4, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 Normalize the grouped variables by their common positive total. The resulting vector is Dirichlet with parameters $(b_1,\ldots,b_r)$ by [F1], while $W_\ell/\sum_hW_h=\sum_{j\in I_\ell}P_j$ by step 1.1. This proves the claim for $r\ge2$. For $r=1$ the only coordinate sum is $\sum_{j=1}^kP_j=1$, which is the stated one-category law. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure, draw $G\sim DP(\alpha)$, and, conditionally on $G$,
draw $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with joint law $G^{\otimes n}$, where $n\ge1$. Then
$$K(x_1,\ldots,x_n;\,\cdot)=DP\!\left(\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}\right)$$
is a measurable data-indexed posterior kernel version. It satisfies the
posterior disintegration identity on the evaluation sigma-algebra of
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ and $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. On prior-predictive
null data sets its values are a version choice; the displayed formula is
well-defined there but is not asserted to be uniquely forced.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; the standard Borel space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$; the finite nonzero measure $\alpha$; and the proper model with prior $DP(\alpha)$ and conditional sample kernel $G\mapsto G^{\otimes n}$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[A2] AC implies Countable Choice, required by the finite-dimensional Dirichlet density normalization and conjugacy theorem. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The sample space is standard Borel, $\alpha$ is finite and nonzero, and $DP(\alpha)$ is the unique law on evaluation-measurable probability measures with its finite-partition Dirichlet laws; cells of zero base mass have mass zero. [[def-standard-borel-space]] [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]] [[def-dirichlet-process]] [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]].

[F2] IID means mutual independence and identical marginal law; the conditional sample kernel is the finite product $G^{\otimes n}$. [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] [[def-independent-random-elements]] [[thm-independent-random-elements-have-product-joint-law]] [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

[F3] A prior probability and a probability sampling kernel define a joint law by kernel integration. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]] [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]].

[F4] A data-indexed posterior kernel is a probability kernel satisfying the joint-law rectangle identity; its values on a data-marginal null set are not fixed by that identity. [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]].

[F5] For positive Dirichlet parameters and an admissible multinomial count vector, the finite-dimensional posterior is Dirichlet with parameters $a_j+y_j$; the evidence is finite positive. The supplier assumes Countable Choice. [[thm-dirichlet-multinomial-conjugate-update]] [[def-dirichlet-distribution]].

[F6] Grouping Dirichlet coordinates adds their parameters. [[lem-dirichlet-aggregation-under-coarsening]].

[F7] Finite measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and the whole space are equal. [[def-pi-system]] [[lem-finite-measure-uniqueness-on-a-pi-system]] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]].

[F8] Each $\delta_x$ is a probability measure, and a finite sum of finite measures with nonnegative coefficients is a measure; hence $\beta_x=\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{x_i}$ is finite and nonzero. [[def-dirac-measure]] [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]] [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]] [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]].

[F9] If $P_j\in\mathcal A$, the indicator $x_i\mapsto\mathbf1_{P_j}(x_i)$ is measurable, so each finite count-pattern fiber is measurable. [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

[F10] Measurable data rectangles form a generating pi-system for the finite product sigma-algebra $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ put $\beta_x=\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. This is a finite nonzero measure because its total mass is $\alpha(\mathsf X)+n$ by [F8]. The existence theorem [F1] therefore defines $DP(\beta_x)$ for every $x$. [A1, given, F1, F8, algebra]

1.2 Fix a finite evaluation cylinder $C=\{G:(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_s))\in H\}$ with Borel $H$, and form the finite Boolean partition generated by $A_1,\ldots,A_s$. On each cell $P_j$, the updated parameter is $\beta_x(P_j)=\alpha(P_j)+\sum_i\mathbf1_{P_j}(x_i)$. Each count is a measurable finite-valued function of $x$ by [F9], so $x\mapsto DP(\beta_x)(C)$ is measurable: it is constant on each of finitely many count-pattern preimages. [F1, F9, given, construct]

1.3 For each $G\in\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$, the map $A\mapsto G(A)$ is a probability kernel from the evaluation-measurable space $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ to $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$. Its finite product $G^{\otimes n}$ is a probability kernel by [F2]; on rectangles $D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$ it has value $\prod_iG(D_i)$, which is evaluation-measurable. The proper model in [F3] therefore gives a joint probability $J$ for $(G,X_{1:n})$ and its data marginal $M$. [F2, F3, given, construct]

1.4 Fix a finite-partition cylinder $C$ and a data rectangle $D=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$. Refine the partition defining $C$ by all $D_i$ to obtain a finite measurable partition $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ of $\mathsf X$. The data rectangle is a disjoint union of ordered cell-pattern blocks $P_{j_1}\times\cdots\times P_{j_n}$. For one such block let $y_j=\#\{i:j_i=j\}$. If $y_j>0$ for a cell with $\alpha(P_j)=0$, then $G(P_j)=0$ almost surely by [F1], so the block has prior-predictive mass zero. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The finite evaluation cylinders form a generating pi-system. The class of sets $C$ for which $x\mapsto DP(\beta_x)(C)$ is measurable contains this pi-system, contains the whole space, is closed under complements, and is closed under countable disjoint unions by pointwise limits of partial sums. Dynkin's theorem [F7] gives measurability on the full evaluation sigma-algebra. Each section is a probability measure by [F1], so $K$ is a probability kernel. [F1, F7, step 1.2, construct]

2.2 Otherwise omit cells with $\alpha(P_j)=0$ (their counts are zero). On the remaining cells the prior vector is Dirichlet with positive parameters $a_j=\alpha(P_j)$. Given that vector, the likelihood of this particular ordered pattern is $\prod_jG(P_j)^{y_j}$, a constant multiple $\prod_jy_j!/n!$ of the multinomial count likelihood. By [A2] and [F5], its posterior vector is Dirichlet$(a_1+y_1,\ldots,a_m+y_m)$ with positive finite evidence. Coarsening to the cells defining $C$ gives the same cylinder probability as $DP(\beta_x)$ by [F6]. This probability is constant over the ordered block because its cell counts are fixed. [A2, F1, F5, F6, step 1.4, algebra]

3.1 Summing step 2.2 over the ordered blocks contained in $D$ gives $J(C\times D)=\int_DK(x,C)\,M(dx)$ for every finite-partition cylinder $C$ and data rectangle $D$. For fixed such $C$, the two sides define finite measures of $D$; their total masses agree by taking $D=\mathsf X^n$. Finite-measure uniqueness [F7] extends the identity to every $D\in\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. [F3, F7, F10, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Now fix any $D\in\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. The set functions $C\mapsto J(C\times D)$ and $C\mapsto\int_DK(x,C)\,M(dx)$ are finite measures on the evaluation sigma-algebra; the second is a measure because $K$ is a probability kernel. They have common total mass $M(D)$ and agree on every finite-partition cylinder by step 3.1. These cylinders form a generating pi-system, so [F7] extends equality to every measurable $C$. By [F4], $K(x;\cdot)$ is the claimed posterior version. Null data blocks contribute zero to both sides, so the proof imposes no pointwise uniqueness there. [F4, F7, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. In the conditionally IID model
$G\sim DP(\alpha)$, $X_i\mid G\sim G$, the posterior version after
$x_{1:n}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ has one-step predictive probability
$$\Pr(X_{n+1}\in A\mid X_{1:n}=x_{1:n})=\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1_A(x_i)}{\alpha(\mathsf X)+n}$$
for every measurable $A$ and every data vector. The formula is a
data-indexed version on prior-predictive null data sets; those pointwise
values are not uniquely determined by the disintegration identity.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; a standard Borel space; finite nonzero $\alpha$; and conditionally IID sampling from $G\sim DP(\alpha)$.

[A1] Full AC is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[A2] AC implies Countable Choice, as required by the Dirichlet-multinomial update. [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]] [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The data-indexed posterior version is $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{x_i})$. [[thm-dirichlet-process-posterior-update]].

[F2] Given the random measure and the observed past, the next observation has conditional probability $G(A)$ of falling in $A$, by the conditionally IID product sampling kernel. [[def-dirichlet-process]] [[def-probability-measure]].

[F3] On every finite partition, positive-base cells have the Dirichlet law and zero-base cells have mass zero. [[def-dirichlet-process]] [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]].

[F4] Under Countable Choice, the one-trial Dirichlet-multinomial evidence for the first cell of a two-cell partition with positive parameters $(b,c)$ is $b/(b+c)$. [[thm-dirichlet-multinomial-conjugate-update]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and $n\ge0$.

1.1 Put $\beta_x=\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. For $n\ge1$, [F1]
makes the posterior law $DP(\beta_x)$; for $n=0$ it is the prior $DP(\alpha)$. In either case, $\beta_x(\mathsf X)=\alpha(\mathsf X)+n>0$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Let $b=\beta_x(A)$ and $c=\beta_x(A^c)$. If $b=0$, [F3] gives $G(A)=0$ almost surely under $DP(\beta_x)$; if $c=0$, it gives $G(A)=1$ almost surely. If both are positive, apply [F4] to one Bernoulli draw on the partition $(A,A^c)$: its probability of the first cell is the Dirichlet-multinomial evidence $b/(b+c)$, which equals $\mathbb E_{DP(\beta_x)}G(A)$ by the sampling kernel [F2]. Thus in all cases the predictive probability is $b/(b+c)=(\alpha(A)+\sum_i\mathbf1_A(x_i))/(\alpha(\mathsf X)+n)$. [A1, A2, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, cases, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The normalized-gamma construction and finite-partition posterior update
state no topology on $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ and specify no density model.
They therefore establish neither a weak-support theorem nor density-posterior
consistency or contraction. Any such conclusion needs its topology, truth
class, prior-mass hypotheses, and a separate posterior-contraction proof.
The finite-dimensional prior-mass bound in Ghosal--van der Vaart is part of
such a separate mixture analysis; it is not a consequence of the conjugate
update alone.

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\mathsf X=\{a,b,c\}$ with its discrete sigma-algebra and
base masses $\alpha(\{a\})=2$, $\alpha(\{b\})=1$, and
$\alpha(\{c\})=1$. For $G\sim DP(\alpha)$, consider two conditionally IID
draws with observed values $X_1=a$, $X_2=b$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite space and base measure in the Example.

[A1] Assume AC, as required by the normalized-gamma and posterior results. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] The finite-partition masses under $DP(\alpha)$ have the Dirichlet law. [[def-dirichlet-process]] [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]].

[F2] After data with cell counts $y_j$, the finite-partition posterior is Dirichlet with parameters $\alpha_j+y_j$. [[thm-dirichlet-process-posterior-update]].

[F3] The next-draw probability in a measurable cell is its base mass plus its observed count, divided by total base mass plus sample size. [[thm-dirichlet-process-polya-urn-predictive-law]].

## Verification

**Given:** The specified three-cell partition, its base masses, and the observed cell sequence $(a,b)$.

1.1 The prior vector $(G(\{a\}),G(\{b\}),G(\{c\}))$ has law $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,1,1)$ by [F1]. The observed counts are $(1,1,0)$, so [F2] gives posterior $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(3,2,1)$, whose parameters sum to $6$. [A1, F1, F2, given]

2.1 Applying [F3] after the two observations gives next-draw probabilities $3/6=1/2$ for $a$, $2/6=1/3$ for $b$, and $1/6$ for $c$; they sum to one. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Before any draw, [F3] gives $\Pr(X_1=a)=2/4=1/2$. After observing $X_1=a$, the same rule gives $\Pr(X_2=a\mid X_1=a)=3/5$. Therefore $\Pr(X_1=a,X_2=a)=(1/2)(3/5)=3/10$: the first draw increases the next draw's mass for its cell from $2/4$ to $3/5$. [F3, algebra] ∎

## Example

Assume AC. Let $\mathsf X=\{a,b\}$ with the discrete sigma-algebra and let
$\alpha=\delta_a$, so $\alpha(\{b\})=0$. In the model
$G\sim DP(\alpha)$ and $X_1\mid G\sim G$, examine the data event
$\{X_1=b\}$.

Separately, let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal B)$ be any standard Borel space, let
$\gamma$ be a finite nonzero diffuse measure (meaning
$\gamma(\{z\})=0$ for every $z\in\mathsf Y$), and fix one $y\in\mathsf Y$.
The verification also checks the posterior-version freedom on this fixed
singleton data fiber.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite space and base measure in the Example.

[A1] Assume AC, as required by the process existence and posterior results. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] A cell with zero base mass has $G$-mass zero almost surely under $DP(\alpha)$. [[def-dirichlet-process]] [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]].

[F2] For every finite nonzero base measure, the normalized-Gamma theorem defines $DP$ and the posterior update gives the measurable kernel $z\mapsto DP(\gamma+\delta_z)$ satisfying disintegration. [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]] [[thm-dirichlet-process-posterior-update]] [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]].

[F3] In a one-draw model with finite nonzero base measure $\beta$, $\Pr(X_1\in A)=\beta(A)/\beta(\mathsf X)$. [[thm-dirichlet-process-polya-urn-predictive-law]].

[F4] In a standard Borel space every singleton is measurable: under a Polish presentation it corresponds to a closed singleton. [[def-standard-borel-space]].

[F5] A probability kernel has probability-measure sections and measurable evaluations; its disintegration identity is checked on measurable rectangles. [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] [[def-probability-measure]] [[def-bayesian-posterior-as-regular-conditional-law]].

## Verification

**Given:** The finite two-point model in the Example and, separately, the standard Borel diffuse-base model $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal B,\gamma)$ with fixed $y\in\mathsf Y$.

1.1 By [F1], $G(\{b\})=0$ almost surely. Since $\Pr(X_1=b\mid G)=G(\{b\})$, integration over the prior gives $\Pr(X_1=b)=0$, also agreeing with [F3]. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 The formula in [F2] assigns $K(b)=DP(\delta_a+\delta_b)$ at the null data value. Define another kernel by $K'(a)=K(a)$ and $K'(b)=DP(\delta_a)$. Both sections are probability measures, and $K'$ is measurable because $\{b\}$ is measurable in the discrete data space. For any measurable event $C$ in $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$, the disintegration integrals for $K$ and $K'$ differ only at $b$, which has data-marginal mass zero by step 1.1. Thus both are posterior versions; the update formula at $b$ is a version choice, not evidence-supported learning. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 In the separate diffuse-base model, [F3] gives data-marginal mass $M(\{y\})=\gamma(\{y\})/\gamma(\mathsf Y)=0$. Let $K(z)=DP(\gamma+\delta_z)$ be the posterior kernel from [F2] and set $K'(z)=K(z)$ for $z\ne y$, $K'(y)=DP(\gamma)$. By [F4], $\{y\}$ is measurable. For every measurable $C\subseteq\mathcal P(\mathsf Y)$, $z\mapsto K'(z,C)=\mathbf1_{\mathsf Y\setminus\{y\}}(z)K(z,C)+\mathbf1_{\{y\}}(z)DP(\gamma)(C)$ is measurable; each section is a probability measure, so [F5] makes $K'$ a probability kernel. The disintegration integrals for $K$ and $K'$ agree on every measurable rectangle because the kernels differ only on $\{y\}$ and $M(\{y\})=0$. Thus $K'$ is also a posterior version, proving that the displayed update value at this fixed null fiber is not uniquely determined. [F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra, construct] ∎
